questions.question:
The security system at an IT office is composed of 10 computers of which exactly four are
working. To check whether the system is functional, the officials inspect four of the
computers picked at random (without replacement). The system is deemed functional if at
least three of the four computers inspected are working. Let the probability that the system is deemed functional be denoted by p.  Then 100p= _____________.
questions.explanation:
4 working, 6 not working. Choose 4 computers: [latex]\binom{10}{4}=210[/latex] ways.

- Exactly 3 working: [latex]\binom43\binom61=24[/latex]
- All 4 working: [latex]\binom44=1[/latex]

[latex]p=\frac{25}{210}=0.119\Rightarrow 100p\approx 11.9[/latex]

Answer: 11.9

questions.question:
Each of the nine words in the sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" is
written on a separate piece of paper. These nine pieces of paper are kept in a box. One of the pieces is drawn at random from the box. The expected length of the word drawn is
_____________. (The answer should be rounded to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Word lengths: The(3), quick(5), brown(5), fox(3), jumps(5), over(4), the(3), lazy(4), dog(3).

[latex]E=\frac{3+5+5+3+5+4+3+4+3}{9}=\frac{35}{9}=3.89\approx 3.9[/latex]

Answer: 3.9

If the matrix A is such that
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ -4\\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &9 &5 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Then the determinant of A is equal to ________.
questions.explanation:
A is a column vector times a row vector, so every row of A is a multiple of [1 9 5]. Hence rank(A) = 1.

A 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 matrix with rank 1 is singular, so det(A) = 0.

questions.question: A non-zero polynomial f(x) of degree 3 has roots at x = 1,x = 2 and x = 3. Which one of the following must be TRUE?

[latex]f(x)=c(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)[/latex] with [latex]c\ne0[/latex].

[latex]f(0)=-6c,\quad f(4)=6c[/latex]
[latex]f(0)f(4)=-36c^2\lt 0[/latex] always (whatever the sign of c), while the sum f(0) + f(4) = 0.

questions.question: The dual of a Boolean function [latex]F(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}, +, \cdot , ' ) [/latex] , written as [latex]F^{D}[/latex], is the same expression as that of F with + and  [latex]\cdot[/latex]  swapped. F is said to be self-dual if [latex]F=F^{D}[/latex].  The number of self-dual functions with n Boolean variables is
questions.explanation:
A self-dual function satisfies [latex]F(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_n)=\overline{F(x_1,\dots,x_n)}[/latex].

The [latex]2^n[/latex] input rows form [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] complementary pairs. Choosing F on one row of a pair fixes F on the other, so we freely choose [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] bits.

Number of self-dual functions = [latex]2^{2^{n-1}}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]2^{2^{n-1}}[/latex]

questions.question: Let  [latex]k = 2^{n}[/latex] . A circuit is built by giving the output of an n-bit binary counter as input to an n-to-[latex]2^{n}[/latex] bit decoder. This circuit is equivalent to a
questions.explanation:
The n-bit counter goes 0, 1, 2, ..., [latex]2^n-1[/latex]. The decoder makes exactly one of its [latex]k=2^n[/latex] outputs 1 for each count.

So the single 1 moves 000..1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 00..10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] ... [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10..0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] back to start. This is exactly a k-bit ring counter.

Answer: k-bit ring counter

questions.question:
A 4-way set-associative cache memory unit with a capacity of 16 KB is built using a block
size of 8 words. The word length is 32 bits. The size of the physical address space is 4 GB.
The number of bits for the TAG field is _____

- Block = 8 words [latex]\times[/latex] 4 B = 32 B [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] offset = 5 bits
- Blocks = 16 KB / 32 B = 512, sets = 512 / 4 = 128 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index = 7 bits
- Address = 4 GB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 32 bits

TAG = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 7 [latex]-[/latex] 5 = 20 bits

Answer: 20

questions.question: Suppose n and p are unsigned int variables in a C program. We wish to set p to [latex]^nC_3[/latex]. If n is large, which one of the following statements is most likely to set p correctly?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)(n[latex]-[/latex]2) is computed first, which overflows for large n.
- Option 2: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)/2 is always an exact integer; multiplying by (n[latex]-[/latex]2) gives a multiple of 3, so /3 is also exact. Intermediate values stay small.
- Option 3: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)/3 need not be exact (e.g. n = 5: 20/3), so truncation gives wrong result.
- Option 4: divides by 2 and then by 6, i.e. by 12 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] wrong.

Answer: p = n * (n - 1) / 2 * (n-2) / 3;

questions.question:
A priority queue is implemented as a Max-Heap. Initially, it has 5 elements. The level-order
traversal of the heap is: 10, 8, 5, 3, 2. Two new elements 1 and 7 are inserted into the heap in
that order. The level-order traversal of the heap after the insertion of the elements is:
questions.explanation:
Heap: 10, 8, 5, 3, 2.

- Insert 1: goes as left child of 5; 1 [latex]\lt[/latex] 5, no swap [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1
- Insert 7: goes as right child of 5; 7 [latex]\gt[/latex] 5, swap; 7 [latex]\lt[/latex] 10, stop [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10, 8, 7, 3, 2, 1, 5

Answer: 10, 8, 7, 3, 2, 1, 5

questions.question:
Consider the tree arcs of a BFS traversal from a source node W in an unweighted, connected,
undirected graph. The tree T formed by the tree arcs is a data structure for computing

options.A: the shortest path between every pair of vertices
options.B: the shortest path from W to every vertex in the graph.
options.C: the shortest paths from W to only those nodes that are leaves of T.
options.D: the longest path in the graph.

questions.explanation:
In an unweighted graph BFS visits vertices level by level from W, so the tree path from W to any vertex v has the minimum number of edges.

It does not give shortest paths between other pairs of vertices.

Answer: the shortest path from W to every vertex in the graph

questions.question:
If [latex]L_{1}=\{a^{n}|n\geq 0\}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}=\{b^{n}|n\geq 0 \}[/latex], Consider
(I) [latex] L_{1}\cdot L_{2}[/latex] is a regular language
(II) [latex] L_{1} \cdot L_{2}= \{a^{n}b^{n}|n \geq 0\}[/latex]
Which one of the following is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
[latex]L_1\cdot L_2=\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}=a^*b^*[/latex], which is regular [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (I) true.

The counts of a and b are independent, so it is not [latex]\{a^nb^n\}[/latex] (e.g. aab is in it) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (II) false.

Answer: Only (I)

questions.question: Let [latex]A \leq _{m}B[/latex] denotes that language A is mapping reducible (also known as many-to-one reducible) to language B. Which one of the following is FALSE?

options.A: If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and B is recursive then A is recursive
options.B: If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and A is undecidable then B is undecidable
options.C: If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and B is recursively enumerable then A is recursively enumerable.
options.D: If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and B is not recursively enumerable then A is not recursively enumerable

questions.explanation:
If [latex]A\le_m B[/latex], A is "no harder" than B. So decidability/RE-ness of B passes down to A, and undecidability of A passes up to B. Options 1, 2, 3 are true.

Option 4 is false: B being non-RE says nothing about A. Example: a decidable language A (non-trivial) reduces to the complement of the halting problem, which is not RE, yet A is RE.

Answer: If [latex]A\le_m B[/latex] and B is not RE then A is not RE

questions.question:
Consider the grammar defined by the following production rules, with two operators * and +
S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex]T *P
T [latex]\rightarrow[/latex]U| T*U
P [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q +P |Q
Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Id
U [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Id
Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: [latex]+[/latex] is left associative, while * is right associative
options.B: [latex]+[/latex] is right associative, while * is left associative

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]T\rightarrow T*U[/latex] is left recursive [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] * is left associative.
- [latex]P\rightarrow Q+P[/latex] is right recursive [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] + is right associative.

Answer: + is right associative, while * is left associative

Dynamic memory allocation (malloc/new) happens only when the program runs.

questions.question: Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: The requirements document also describes how the requirements that are listed in the document are implemented efficiently.
options.B:
Consistency and completeness of functional requirements are always achieved in
practice.
options.C: Prototyping is a method of requirements validation
options.D: Requirements review is carried out to find the errors in system design

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- The requirements document says what the system should do, not how it is implemented.
- Complete and consistent requirements are rarely achieved in practice.
- Prototyping lets users check the requirements early, so it is a requirements validation technique [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True.
- Requirements review finds errors in the requirements, not in the design.

questions.question:
A FAT (file allocation table) based file system is being used and the total overhead of each
entry in the FAT is 4 bytes in size. Given a 100x[latex]10^{6}[/latex] bytes disk on which the file system is
stored and data block size is [latex]10^{3}[/latex] bytes, the maximum size of a file that can be stored on this
disk in units of [latex]10^{6}[/latex] bytes is _______.
questions.explanation:
Number of blocks = [latex]\frac{100\times10^6}{10^3}=10^5[/latex], one FAT entry per block.

FAT size = [latex]10^5\times4=0.4\times10^6[/latex] bytes.

Max file size = [latex](100-0.4)\times10^6=99.6\times10^6[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 99.6

questions.question:
Which one of the following is TRUE about the interior gateway routing protocols - Routing
Information Protocol (RIP) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)?

options.A: RIP uses distance vector routing and OSPF uses link state routing
options.B: OSPF uses distance vector routing and RIP uses link state routing
options.C: Both RIP and OSPF use link state routing
options.D: Both RIP and OSPF use distance vector routing

RIP shares distance vectors with neighbours (Bellman-Ford). OSPF floods link-state advertisements and runs Dijkstra.

Answer: RIP uses distance vector routing and OSPF uses link state routing

The links within each ISP and across the two ISPs, are all point-to-point' optical links. The initial value of the TTL field is 32. questions.question: Consider the store and forward packet switched network given below. Assume that the bandwidth of each link is [latex]10^{6}[/latex] bytes / sec. A user on host A sends a file of size [latex]10^{3}[/latex] bytes to host B through routers R1 and R2 in three different ways. In the first case a single packet containing the complete file is transmitted from A to B. In the second case, the file is split into 10 equal parts, and these packets are transmitted from A to B. In the third case, the file is split into 20 equal parts and these packets are sent from A to B. Each packet contains 100 bytes of header information along with the user data. Consider only transmission time and ignore processing, queuing and propagation delays. Also assume that there are no errors during transmission. Let T1, T2 and T3 be the times taken to transmit the file in the first, second and third case respectively. Which one of the following is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
Rate = [latex]10^6[/latex] B/s, so 1 byte takes 1 [latex]\mu s[/latex]. There are 3 links (A[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]B). With pipelining, time = (packets + 2) [latex]\times[/latex] one-packet time.

- T1: 1 packet of 1000 + 100 = 1100 B [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 1100 = 3300 [latex]\mu s[/latex]
- T2: 10 packets of 100 + 100 = 200 B [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 12 [latex]\times[/latex] 200 = 2400 [latex]\mu s[/latex]
- T3: 20 packets of 50 + 100 = 150 B [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 22 [latex]\times[/latex] 150 = 3300 [latex]\mu s[/latex]

Answer: T1 = T3, T3 [latex]\gt[/latex] T2

questions.question:
An IP machine Q has a path to another IP machine H via three IP routers R1, R2, and R3.
Q---R1---R2---R3---H
H acts as an HTTP server, and Q connects to H via HTTP and downloads a file. Session layer encryption is used, with DES as the shared key encryption protocol. Consider the following four pieces of information:
[I1] The URL of the file downloaded by Q
[I2] The TCP port numbers at Q and H
[I3] The IP addresses of Q and H
[I4] The link layer addresses of Q and H
Which of I1, I2, I3, and I4 can an intruder learn through sniffing at R2 alone?
questions.explanation:
Session-layer encryption hides everything above the session layer (the HTTP request, so the URL I1 is hidden).

- TCP header (ports, I2) and IP header (addresses of Q and H, I3) are below it and travel in clear [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] visible at R2.
- Link layer addresses change at every hop; at R2 the frame carries the MACs of R1/R2/R3, not of Q and H [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] I4 not visible.

Answer: Only I2 and I3

questions.question:
A graphical HTML browser resident at a network client machine Q accesses a static HTML
webpage from a HTTP server S. The static HTML page has exactly one static embedded
image which is also at S. Assuming no caching, which one of the following is correct about
the HTML webpage loading (including the embedded image)?

options.A:
Q needs to send at least 2 HTTP requests to S, each necessarily in a separate TCP
connection to server S
options.B: Q needs to send at least 2 HTTP requests to S, but a single TCP connection to server S is sufficient
options.C: A single HTTP request from Q to S is sufficient, and a single TCP connection between Q and S is necessary for this
options.D: A single HTTP request from Q to S is sufficient, and this is possible without any TCP connection between Q and S

questions.explanation:
The HTML page and the embedded image are two separate objects, so at least 2 HTTP GET requests are needed.

With persistent HTTP (keep-alive), both requests can be sent over one TCP connection.

Answer: Q needs to send at least 2 HTTP requests to S, but a single TCP connection is sufficient

questions.question:
Consider a join (relation algebra) between relations r(R)and s(S) using the nested loop
method. There are 3 buffers each of size equal to disk block size, out of which one buffer is
reserved for intermediate results. Assuming size(r(R))[latex]\lt[/latex]size(s(S)), the join will have fewer
number of disk block accesses if

options.A: relation r(R) is in the outer loop.
options.B: relation s(S) is in the outer loop
options.C: join selection factor between r(R) and s(S) is more than 0.5.
options.D: join selection factor between r(R) and s(S) is less than 0.5

questions.explanation:
With one buffer each for the outer and inner relation, block accesses = [latex]b_{outer}+b_{outer}\times b_{inner}[/latex].

The product term is the same either way, so the cost is smaller when the outer relation has fewer blocks. Since r is smaller, put r in the outer loop.

Answer: relation r(R) is in the outer loop

questions.question:
Consider the procedure below for the Producer-Consumer problem which uses semaphores:

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: The producer will be able to add an item to the buffer, but the consumer can never consume it.
options.B: The consumer will remove no more than one item from the buffer.
options.C: Deadlock occurs if the consumer succeeds in acquiring semaphore s when the buffer is empty
options.D: The starting value for the semaphore n must be 1 and not 0 for deadlock-free operation.

questions.explanation:
The consumer does semWait(s) before semWait(n).

If the buffer is empty (n = 0) and the consumer gets s first, it blocks on n while holding s. The producer then blocks on semWait(s) and can never signal n [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock.

Answer: Deadlock occurs if the consumer succeeds in acquiring semaphore s when the buffer is empty

questions.question:
Three processes A, B and C each execute a loop of 100 iterations. In each iteration of the loop, a process performs a single computation that requires [latex]t_{c}[/latex] CPU milliseconds and then initiates a single I/O operation that lasts for [latex]t_{io}[/latex] milliseconds. It is assumed that the computer where the processes execute has sufficient number of I/O devices and the OS of the computer assigns different I/O devices to each process. Also, the scheduling overhead of the OS is negligible. The processes have the following characteristics:

The processes A, B, and C are started at times 0, 5 and 10 milliseconds respectively, in a pure time sharing system (round robin scheduling) that uses a time slice of 50 milliseconds. The time in milliseconds at which process C would complete its first I/O operation is ___________.
questions.explanation:

- 0-50 A, 50-100 B, 100-150 C, 150-200 A (A done, goes to I/O)
- 200-250 B, 250-300 C, 300-350 B, 350-400 C
- 400-450 B, 450-500 C (C done with 200 ms)

C starts I/O at 500 and finishes it at 500 + 500 = 1000 ms.

Answer: 1000

questions.question:
A computer has twenty physical page frames which contain pages numbered 101 through
120. Now a program accesses the pages numbered 1, 2, ..., 100 in that order, and repeats the
access sequence THRICE. Which one of the following page replacement policies experiences
the same number of page faults as the optimal page replacement policy for this program?
questions.explanation:
The pages 1..100 are accessed in a cycle, and memory holds only 20.

LRU and FIFO always evict the page that will be needed soonest in a cyclic pattern, so they fault on every access. Optimal evicts the page used farthest in future, which is the most recently used page.

So MRU behaves exactly like the optimal policy here.

Answer: Most-recently-used

t2 = k * 4

Then, L is
questions.explanation:

questions.question:
Let [latex]L_{1}=\{w \in \{0,1\}*|w[/latex] has at least as many occurrences of (110)'s as (011)'s}.
Let [latex]L_{2}=\{w \in \{0,1\}*|w[/latex] has at least as many occurrence of (000)'s as (111)'s}.

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: L1 is regular but not L2
options.B: L2 is regular but not L1
options.C: Both L1 and L2 are regular
options.D: Neither L1 nor L2 are regular

questions.explanation:
L1: 110 and 011 occurrences alternate in a binary string, so their counts differ by at most 1, depending only on how the string starts and ends. A finite automaton can check this [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] regular.

L2: counts of 000 and 111 can grow independently (e.g. [latex]0^n1^n[/latex] type strings), and comparing them needs unbounded counting [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not regular.

Answer: L1 is regular but not L2

questions.question:
Consider two strings A="qpqrr" and B="pqprqrp". Let x be the length of the longest
common subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) between A and B and let y be the number
of such longest common subsequences between A and B. Then x + 10y = ___.
questions.explanation:
A = qpqrr, B = pqprqrp.

The LCS length is x = 4, and the LCSs are: qpqr, qprr, pqrr [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] y = 3.

x + 10y = 4 + 30 = 34

Answer: 34

questions.question:
Suppose P, Q, R, S, T are sorted sequences having lengths 20, 24, 30, 35, 50 respectively.
They are to be merged into a single sequence by merging together two sequences at a time.
The number of comparisons that will be needed in the worst case by the optimal algorithm for doing this is ____.
questions.explanation:
Merging lists of size m and n needs m + n [latex]-[/latex] 1 comparisons in the worst case. Optimal: always merge the two smallest (like Huffman).

- 20 + 24 = 44 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 43
- 30 + 35 = 65 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 64
- 44 + 50 = 94 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 93
- 65 + 94 = 159 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 158

Total = 43 + 64 + 93 + 158 = 358

Answer: 358

questions.question: Consider the expression tree shown. Each leaf represents a numerical value, which can either be 0 or 1. Over all possible choices of the values at the leaves, the maximum possible value of the expression represented by the tree is ___.

Root = (left subtree) + (right subtree).

- Left: (a + b) [latex]-[/latex] (c [latex]-[/latex] d). Max = (1 + 1) [latex]-[/latex] (0 [latex]-[/latex] 1) = 3
- Right: (e [latex]-[/latex] f) + (g + h). Max = (1 [latex]-[/latex] 0) + (1 + 1) = 3

Maximum = 3 + 3 = 6

Answer: 6

questions.question:
Suppose a stack implementation supports an instruction REVERSE, which reverses the order
of elements on the stack, in addition to the PUSH and POP instructions. Which one of the
following statements is TRUE with respect to this modified stack?

options.A: A queue cannot be implemented using this stack.
options.B:
A queue can be implemented where ENQUEUE takes a single instruction and
DEQUEUE takes a sequence of two instructions.
options.C:
A queue can be implemented where ENQUEUE takes a sequence of three instructions
and DEQUEUE takes a single instruction
options.D:
A queue can be implemented where both ENQUEUE and DEQUEUE take a single
instruction each.

questions.explanation:
Keep the front of the queue at the top of the stack.

- ENQUEUE(x): REVERSE, PUSH x, REVERSE (3 instructions)
- DEQUEUE: POP (1 instruction)

Answer: ENQUEUE takes three instructions and DEQUEUE takes one

questions.question:
In designing a computer's cache system, the cache block (or cache line) size is an important
Parameter. Which one of the following statements is correct in this context?

options.A: A smaller block size implies better spatial locality
options.B: A smaller block size implies a smaller cache tag and hence lower cache tag overhead
options.C: A smaller block size implies a larger cache tag and hence lower cache hit time
options.D: A smaller block size incurs a lower cache miss penalty

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Smaller blocks bring fewer neighbouring words, so spatial locality is used less.
- Smaller blocks mean more blocks [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] more tags overall, i.e. more tag overhead.
- On a miss only a small block is transferred, so miss penalty is lower [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True.

Answer: A smaller block size incurs a lower cache miss penalty

questions.question:
If the associativity of a processor cache is doubled while keeping the capacity and block size
unchanged, which one of the following is guaranteed to be NOT affected?

options.D: Width of processor to main memory data bus

questions.explanation:
Doubling associativity halves the number of sets: the index loses 1 bit, the tag gains 1 bit, and the way multiplexer gets twice the inputs.

The processor-to-memory data bus width does not depend on cache organisation.

Answer: Width of processor to main memory data bus

- Exponent = 3 + 127 = 130 = 10000010
- Mantissa = 1100100...0

questions.question:
In the Newton-Raphson method, an initial guess of [latex]x_{0}=2[/latex] is made and the sequence [latex]x_{0},x_{1},x_{2}...[/latex] is obtained for the function
[latex]0.75x^{3}-2x^{2}-2x+4=0[/latex]
Consider the statements
(I) [latex]x_{3}[/latex]=0.
(II) The method converges to a solution in a finite number of iterations.
Which of the following is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
[latex]f(x)=0.75x^3-2x^2-2x+4,\quad f'(x)=2.25x^2-4x-2[/latex]

- [latex]x_0=2[/latex]: f = [latex]-[/latex]2, f' = [latex]-[/latex]1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]x_1=2-\frac{-2}{-1}=0[/latex]
- [latex]x_1=0[/latex]: f = 4, f' = [latex]-[/latex]2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]x_2=0-\frac{4}{-2}=2[/latex]

The values repeat 2, 0, 2, 0, ... so [latex]x_3=0[/latex] (I true), and the method never converges (II false).

Answer: Only I

questions.question:
Consider the following relation on subsets of the set S of integers between 1 and 2014. For two distinct subsets U and V of S we say U[latex]\lt[/latex]V if the minimum element in the symmetric difference of the two sets is in U.
Consider the following two statements:
S1: There is a subset of S that is larger than every other subset.
S2: There is a subset of S that is smaller than every other subset.
Which one of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are true
options.B: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.C: S2 is true and S1 is false
options.D: Neither S1 nor S2 is true

questions.explanation:
U [latex]\lt[/latex] V when the smallest element of [latex]U\triangle V[/latex] lies in U.

- Take U = S (the full set). For any V [latex]\ne[/latex] S, [latex]S\triangle V=S-V[/latex], whose minimum is in S. So S is smaller than every other subset [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S2 true.
- Take V = [latex]\emptyset[/latex]. For any U, [latex]U\triangle\emptyset=U[/latex], minimum in U, so U [latex]\lt\emptyset[/latex]. So [latex]\emptyset[/latex] is larger than every other subset [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S1 true.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true

questions.question: A cycle on n vertices is isomorphic to its complement. The value of n is _____.
questions.explanation:
A cycle [latex]C_n[/latex] has n edges, its complement has [latex]\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-n[/latex] edges. Isomorphic graphs have equal edge counts:
[latex]n=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-n\Rightarrow n=5[/latex]

Indeed the complement of [latex]C_5[/latex] (the pentagram) is again a 5-cycle.

Answer: 5

questions.question: The number of distinct minimum spanning trees for the weighted graph below is
questions.explanation:
Use Kruskal. All weight-1 edges are taken (they form no cycle), leaving components: {top-left, centre, left, bottom}, {top-right, right}, {triangle edge pair of weight 1}, {triangle's bottom-left vertex}.

Now weight-2 edges:
- Join the two left components: 3 choices (top edge, centre-top-right, centre-right).
- The long bottom edge is the only link to the triangle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] forced.
- Join the triangle's last vertex: 2 choices (either weight-2 edge of the triangle).

Number of MSTs = 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 6

Answer: 6

questions.question:
SQL allows duplicate tuples in relations, and correspondingly defines the multiplicity of tuples in the result of joins. Which one of the following queries always gives the same answer as the nested query shown below:
Select * from R where a in (select S. a from S)

options.A: Select R. * from R, S where R. a=S. a
options.B: Select distinct R. * from R,S where R. a=S. a
options.C: Select R. * from R, (select distinct a from S) as S1 where R. a=S1.a
options.D: Select R. * from R, S where R.a = S. a and is unique R

questions.explanation:
The IN query returns each R tuple once per its own copy in R, no matter how many matching tuples S has.

- Option 1: a plain join repeats an R tuple once for every matching S tuple [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] extra duplicates.
- Option 2: DISTINCT also removes duplicates that were genuinely in R.
- Option 3: S1 has each value of a only once, so every R tuple matches at most once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] same result.

Answer: Select R.* from R, (select distinct a from S) as S1 where R.a = S1.a

questions.question:
Consider a main memory system that consists of 8 memory modules attached to the system
bus, which is one word wide. When a write request is made, the bus is occupied for 100
nanoseconds (ns) by the data, address, and control signals. During the same 100 ns, and for
500 ns thereafter, the addressed memory module executes one cycle accepting and storing the data. The (internal) operation of different memory modules may overlap in time, but only one request can be on the bus at any time. The maximum number of stores (of one word each) that can be initiated in 1 millisecond is ____________
questions.subtopic: ALU Data Path and Control Unit
questions.explanation:
Each store holds the bus for 100 ns, and a module is busy for 600 ns. With 8 modules used in turn, a module is reused only after 8 [latex]\times[/latex] 100 = 800 ns [latex]\gt[/latex] 600 ns, so modules never cause waiting.

The bus is the bottleneck: one store per 100 ns.

[latex]\frac{1\,ms}{100\,ns}=\frac{10^{-3}}{10^{-7}}=10^4[/latex]

Answer: 10000

questions.question:
Number of people diagnosed with dengue fever (contracted from the bite of a mosquito) in North India is twice the number diagnosed last year. Municipal authorities have concluded that measures to control the mosquito population have failed in this region.

Which one of the following statements, if true, does not contradict this conclusion?

options.A: A high proportion of the affected population has returned from neighbouring countries where dengue is prevalent
options.B: More cases of dengue are now reported because of an increase in the Municipal Office's administrative efficiency
options.C: Many more cases of dengue are being diagnosed this year since the introduction of a new and effective diagnostic test
options.D: The number of people with malarial fever (also contracted from mosquito bites) has increased this year

questions.explanation:
Options 1, 2, 3 give other reasons for more dengue cases (imported cases, better reporting, better diagnosis), so they weaken the conclusion.

More malaria (also mosquito-borne) supports that mosquito control failed, so it does not contradict it.

Answer: The number of people with malarial fever has increased this year
